Markov-chain removal effects

Source: R/markov.R
markov_removal.Rd

Data-driven attribution from a first-order Markov model of the journey table (Anderl, Becker, von Wangenheim and Schumann, 2016). Journeys are treated as walks from a start state through channel states to one of two absorbing states, conversion or null. A channel's removal effect is the proportional drop in the probability of reaching conversion when every transition into that channel is redirected to the null state; conversions are then divided among channels in proportion to their removal effects.

Usage

markov_removal(paths)

Arguments

paths

An mm_paths object from build_paths(). Keep the non-converting journeys (keep_null_paths = TRUE, the default): they are what the null state is estimated from.

Value

A data frame with one row per channel, ordered by descending conversions: channel, removal_effect, conversions (credited), share, value when the journey table carries conversion values, and p_without, the probability of conversion once the channel is removed. Three attributes let you check the removal effects by hand:

p_conversion

The baseline conversion probability. removal_effect is 1 - p_without / p_conversion, or 0 when no journey converts.

transitions

The fitted first-order transition matrix, with one row for each state a walk can leave ("(start)" and every channel) and one column for each state it can enter (every channel, "(conversion)" and "(null)"). Each row sums to 1.

transition_counts

The transitions observed, in the same layout, from which transitions is estimated.

A zero-row journey table gives a zero-row result without these attributes.

Details

The probabilities come from the absorbing-chain fundamental matrix, so they are exact for the fitted transition matrix rather than simulated: with \(Q\) the transitions among transient states and \(R\) those into the absorbing states, absorption probabilities are \((I - Q)^{-1} R\). One inverse serves every channel. Once channel \(s\) is removed, a walk converts only if it converts without reaching \(s\), so with \(N = (I - Q)^{-1}\) and \(x = N R\) the conversion probability is \(x_1 - (N_{1s} / N_{ss}) x_s\), where \(N_{1s} / N_{ss}\) is the probability of ever reaching \(s\) from the start and \(x_s\) that of converting from \(s\). That probability is the p_without column.

A channel named "(start)", "(conversion)" or "(null)" shares its label with a special state in transitions; index the matrix by position in that case.

This is the order-1 model, with no dependency beyond base R. For higher-order chains, or journey tables with millions of distinct paths, hand the output of as_channel_paths() to ChannelAttribution, whose markov_model() implements the same removal-effect definition in C++. For order = 1 the two agree up to the error of ChannelAttribution's simulation.

Removal effects are sensitive to journey construction: repeats collapsed or not, direct traffic kept or dropped, lookback length. That is the argument for build_paths() making each an explicit choice.

What this is not

A removal effect is a statement about the fitted transition matrix, not about what customers would do if a channel were switched off. Removing a state from a chain assumes that everyone who would have passed through it is lost, and that nobody reaches the same conversion another way. It is a more data-driven convention than first- or last-touch, and it is still a convention. Use it alongside the heuristic rules in attribute(), where the spread between them is the honest summary, and use experiments for incrementality.

References

Anderl, E., Becker, I., von Wangenheim, F. and Schumann, J. H. (2016). Mapping the customer journey: Lessons learned from graph-based online attribution modeling. International Journal of Research in Marketing, 33(3), 457–474. doi:10.1016/j.ijresmar.2016.03.001

See also

attribute(), which includes this as the "markov" rule, as_channel_paths() for ChannelAttribution.

Examples

# A three-journey example small enough to check by hand: P(conversion) is
# 2/3; removing "a" halves it, removing "b" makes conversion impossible.
ev <- data.frame(
  id = c("j1", "j1", "j2", "j3"),
  ch = c("a", "b", "a", "b"),
  ts = c(1, 2, 1, 1),
  conv = c(0, 1, 0, 1)
)
p <- build_paths(ev, id = "id", channel = "ch", timestamp = "ts",
                 conversion = "conv")
mk <- markov_removal(p)
mk
#>   channel removal_effect conversions     share p_without
#> 1       b            1.0   1.3333333 0.6666667 0.0000000
#> 2       a            0.5   0.6666667 0.3333333 0.3333333

# The fitted chain behind those numbers
attr(mk, "transitions")
#>          to
#> from              a         b (conversion) (null)
#>   (start) 0.6666667 0.3333333            0    0.0
#>   a       0.0000000 0.5000000            0    0.5
#>   b       0.0000000 0.0000000            1    0.0
attr(mk, "p_conversion")
#> [1] 0.6666667
1 - mk$p_without / attr(mk, "p_conversion")
#> [1] 1.0 0.5

data(mm_events)
paths <- build_paths(mm_events, id = "customer_id", channel = "channel",
                     timestamp = "timestamp", conversion = "conversion",
                     value = "value")
markov_removal(paths)
